cards.headline: The Socratic method
lines: Socrates taught by asking questions rather than giving answers.
Each question tests a belief for hidden contradictions.
The goal is clearer thinking — and admitting what you don't know.
cards.source: Plato's dialogues, e.g. 'Euthyphro' and 'Apology'; Vlastos, 'Socrates: Ironist and Moral Philosopher'.

cards.headline: Stoicism: work on what's up to you
lines: The Stoics split the world into what is up to us — our judgements and actions — and what isn't.
Epictetus taught that we are disturbed not by events, but by our views of them.
Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, wrote his Meditations as notes to himself.

cards.headline: The trolley problem
lines: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever, diverting it to kill one.
Most people say they'd pull it — far fewer would push someone off a bridge to stop it.
The gap suggests we care how harm happens, not only how much.
cards.source: Foot (1967), Oxford Review; Thomson (1985), Yale Law Journal; Greene et al. (2001), Science.

cards.headline: Occam's razor
lines: Don't add assumptions you don't need.
When two explanations fit the evidence equally well, start with the simpler one — then test it.
It's a rule of thumb, not a proof: sometimes the truth is complicated.
cards.source: Attributed to William of Ockham (14th century); Baker, 'Simplicity', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

cards.headline: Plato's cave
lines: Prisoners see only shadows on a wall and take them for reality.
One escapes, sees the sun, and returns — but the others don't believe him.
Plato's point: education turns us toward what's real, and that can be uncomfortable.

cards.question: Who wrote 'I think, therefore I am'?
cards.why: Descartes, in 1637. Doubting everything, he found one thing he couldn't doubt: that he was thinking.
cards.source: Descartes, 'Discourse on the Method' (1637), Part IV.

cards.question: Which view judges actions by whether they produce the greatest good for the greatest number?
cards.why: Associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill: consequences make an action right or wrong.
cards.source: Mill, 'Utilitarianism' (1863); Bentham, 'An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789).

cards.question: According to the Stoics, what is fully within your control?
cards.why: Epictetus: our opinions, intentions and desires are up to us; body, property and reputation are not.

cards.question: Aristotle saw courage as the middle point between…
cards.why: His 'golden mean': a virtue sits between a deficiency and an excess.

cards.question: Occam's razor recommends…
cards.why: When rival explanations fit equally well, the one with fewer assumptions is the better starting point.

cards.headline: Socrates never wrote anything down
cards.text: We know his ideas mainly through his students — above all Plato — and through the historian Xenophon.
cards.source: Kraut, 'Socrates', Encyclopaedia Britannica; Plato's and Xenophon's Socratic writings.

cards.headline: Confucius taught a version of the Golden Rule
cards.text: In the Analects, around 500 BCE: 'What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others.'

cards.headline: Plato founded a school that lasted centuries
cards.text: Plato's Academy in Athens, founded around 387 BCE, is often called the first institution of higher learning in the Western world.

cards.headline: The Ship of Theseus
cards.text: If every plank of a ship is replaced over time, is it still the same ship? Plutarch recorded the puzzle; philosophers still argue about identity.

steps.headline: 1 · Premises and conclusion
lines: An argument gives reasons (premises) for a claim (the conclusion).
First, find what's being claimed — and why.

steps.headline: 2 · Valid
lines: Valid means: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
'All birds have feathers. A robin is a bird. So a robin has feathers.'

steps.headline: 3 · Sound
lines: A sound argument is valid AND its premises really are true.
Valid logic built on a false premise can still reach a false conclusion.

steps.headline: 4 · Watch for fallacies
lines: Attacking the person instead of the point is an ad hominem.
Offering only two options when there are more is a false dilemma.

cards.headline: Philosophy: the takeaways
points: Stoics: focus on what's up to you.
Start with the simpler explanation — then test it.
Plato's cave: learning means turning toward the real.
